summary: This RFC specifies a common, reusable YANG data model for attachment circuits, giving consistent AC structures among models that manipulate them, for example service models exposing ACs.

eli5.summary: A shared building block for describing the link between customer and provider, so other models do not each invent their own.

questions: what is a bearer in yang ac models
subtitle: A shared YANG building block so every model that describes customer-to-provider links uses the same structures.

tldr.problem: Several service, network and device models need to describe attachment circuits, the provisioned links between customer equipment and a provider network, and each could invent its own incompatible structures.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9833 defines the ietf-ac-common YANG module, a library of features, identities and reusable groupings covering Layer 2 and Layer 3 settings, routing, authentication, profiles and bandwidth.
tldr.outcome: Other modules import it, so AC data stays consistent and is easy to pass from service models to network models. The module itself exposes no writable data nodes, state or RPCs.

today: RFC 9833 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2025. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The related models are in RFC 9834, RFC 9835 and RFC 9836.

sections.title: Attachment Circuits and the Need for a Common Model
sections.content:
Networks offer connectivity services to customers through terminating points such as Customer Premises Equipment, Autonomous System Border Routers or data center gateways. For data to flow, the links from the customer's terminating points to the provider network (typically a Provider Edge, PE) must be provisioned. The RFC calls this provisioning an attachment circuit (AC) and the underlying link the bearer.

A service can use existing ACs or need new ones, and ACs can be dedicated to one service or shared. Multiple customer edges can attach to a PE over the same AC, and a single customer edge can terminate several ACs.

This document specifies the ietf-ac-common module so that modules that handle ACs share consistent structures. Examples given are service models exposing AC as a Service (RFC 9834), network models that provision ACs (RFC 9835), and device models. It also eases inheritance of data from service to network models, as in RFC 8969, and conforms to the Network Management Datastore Architecture (RFC 8342).
sections.eli5: An attachment circuit is the set-up of the road from a customer's building to the provider's network. This RFC gives everyone one common way to write that set-up down.

sections.title: Terminology: The Bearer
sections.content:
The one term the RFC defines is bearer: a physical or logical link that connects a customer edge (or site) to a provider network. It can be wireless or wired and built from one or several technologies. The operator allocates a unique bearer reference, for example a customer line identifier, which a customer can later use in service requests to say exactly where a service is to be bound.

One or more ACs can be hosted over the same bearer, for example several VLANs on one physical link. The document also uses the shorthand LxSM for the L2VPN and L3VPN Service Models (RFC 8466, RFC 8299) and LxNM for the L2VPN and L3VPN Network Models (RFC 9291, RFC 9182). Tree diagram symbols come from RFC 8340.
sections.eli5: The bearer is the actual cable or wireless link. Several separate connections, the attachment circuits, can share one cable, like several phone calls on one line.

sections.title: How the AC Models Fit Together
sections.content:
The common module is one of five related modules: ietf-ac-common, ietf-bearer-svc and ietf-ac-svc (both from RFC 9834), ietf-ac-ntw (RFC 9835) and ietf-ac-glue (RFC 9836).

The common module is imported by the bearer, service and network modules. A bearer managed through the bearer module can be referenced by service ACs, and can list the ACs that use it. The network module uses the AC references exposed by the service module so a service request can be correlated with what was provisioned. The glue module augments the L2VPN and L3VPN service and network models with those AC references, binding VPN services to ACs.
sections.eli5: The common module is the shared toolbox. The other four modules each borrow from it, and one more module, the glue, ties them to the VPN models.

sections.title: Features and Identities
sections.content:
The module defines three YANG features: layer2-ac and layer3-ac, indicating support for ACs with Layer 2 or Layer 3 properties, and server-assigned-reference, indicating that a server (such as a controller or router) generates references. With the last, a bearer request created with a client-assigned name also gets a server-generated reference that can be used when requesting an AC over that bearer.

Its identities include types for IP address allocation (for example whether the provider offers DHCP, DHCP relay or static addressing, with SLAAC possible for IPv6), next-hop actions such as discarding traffic, Layer 2 tunnel selection (pseudowire, VPLS, VXLAN), Layer 3 tunnel selection (IP-in-IP, IPsec, GRE), redundancy precedence (to tag primary and secondary ACs), the AC role (UNI, NNI or public NNI) and the BGP role for sessions per RFC 9234.

It also adds four administrative status types on top of those from RFC 9181, shown in the table below.
sections.eli5: Features say what a device can do, and identities are a list of named choices, like picking Primary or Secondary for a link. The module also adds some new labels for where a request is in its approval.

sections.title: Reusable Groupings for Layer 2 and Layer 3
sections.content:
A YANG grouping is a reusable chunk of data model. The module provides service-status (administrative status that is set, operational status that is reported), op-instructions (requested and actual start and stop times) and ac-profile-cfg, a set of valid provider profile identifiers for encryption, QoS, failure detection (such as BFD policies), forwarding (such as ACLs) and routing (such as BGP policies).

For Layer 2, there are groupings for the encapsulations dot1q, qinq and priority-tagged, and for Layer 2 tunnel services: pseudowire, VPLS and VXLAN. For Layer 3, there are IPv4 and IPv6 groupings for address allocation and connections, with basic and more elaborate variants. They support dynamic addressing, including DHCP service or relay with customer DHCP servers, and static addresses. When the allocation type is slaac, Router Advertisements carry the IPv6 prefix determined by local-address and prefix-length.
sections.eli5: A grouping is a ready-made form with some boxes already on it. One form is for Layer 2 settings like VLAN tags, another is for Layer 3 settings like IP addresses.

sections.title: Routing, Authentication and Bandwidth Groupings
sections.content:
Besides static routing, the module supports BGP, OSPF, IS-IS and RIP. For each, an address-family says whether IPv4, IPv6 or both are activated. There are groupings for BGP peer groups (local ASN, customer ASN, address families, optional name and role), basic OSPF and IS-IS parameters, IPv4 and IPv6 static routes, a bfd hold time and a redundancy-group list used to express redundancy or protection constraints.

Authentication groupings exist for BGP, OSPF, IS-IS and RIP. They let a user refer to a key chain (RFC 8177) or supply an explicit key and algorithm for legacy implementations. TCP-AO parameters are assumed to be preconfigured in the referenced key chain. The model covers OSPF authentication common to OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 and so does not support RFC 4552.

Bandwidth can be expressed with the Committed Information Rate (CIR), Excess Information Rate (EIR) or Peak Information Rate (PIR), with burst sizes, per bandwidth type taken from RFC 9181, for example per Class of Service or per site.
sections.eli5: These forms cover how traffic finds its way, the passwords between routers, and how much speed the customer is promised.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is designed to be accessed through YANG-based protocols such as NETCONF (RFC 6241) and RESTCONF, which have to use a secure transport and mutual authentication. The Network Configuration Access Control Model (RFC 8341) can restrict users to a subset of operations and content.

Because the module only defines identities, types and groupings, it exposes no writable data nodes, read-only state or RPCs, so it adds no security issues by itself. Modules that reuse the groupings must state their own security considerations. For example, groupings like ipv6-lan-prefixes or ipv4-lan-prefixes can expose privacy-related information, and disclosing it may violate the customer-provider trust relationship.

The authentication groupings inherit the considerations of RFC 8177. They accept explicit keys as ASCII strings. Hexadecimal keys would give more key entropy per octet but are not included because underlying device modules do not support them.
sections.eli5: The toolbox itself is harmless, but whatever you build with it must be protected. Be careful not to show a customer's private network details to people who should not see them.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA has registered the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-ac-common in the IETF XML Registry. It has also registered the YANG module ietf-ac-common in the YANG Module Names registry, with prefix ac-common, and the registrant contact for the namespace is the IESG. The module itself is revision 2025-09-29 and is published in Section 5 of the RFC, with its full tree in Appendix A.
sections.eli5: The module's name and address were written in the official list so nobody else uses them.
